claim: APOBEC3B (A3B)-catalyzed DNA cytosine deamination contributes to the overall mutational landscape in breast cancer.
source: APOBEC3B (A3B)-catalyzed DNA cytosine deamination contributes to the overall mutational landscape in breast cancer.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about A3B's role in cancer.

claim: A single E2F cis-element mediates repression of A3B in normal cells.
source: Here we show that a single E2F cis-element mediates repression in normal cells and that expression is activated by its mutational disruption in a reporter construct or the endogenous A3B gene.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study demonstrated through reporter assays and CRISPR/Cas9 experiments.

claim: Mutational disruption of the E2F site activates A3B expression in a reporter construct.
source: Here we show that a single E2F cis-element mediates repression in normal cells and that expression is activated by its mutational disruption in a reporter construct or the endogenous A3B gene.
evidence: This is demonstrated through luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mutational disruption of the E2F site activates endogenous A3B gene expression.
source: Here we show that a single E2F cis-element mediates repression in normal cells and that expression is activated by its mutational disruption in a reporter construct or the endogenous A3B gene.
evidence: This is demonstrated through CRISPR/Cas9-mediated HDR experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The E2F site is required for A3B induction by polyomavirus T antigen.
source: The same E2F site is required for A3B induction by polyomavirus T antigen indicating a shared molecular mechanism.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experiments showing that E2F site mutations prevent tTAg-mediated induction.

claim: Wildtype E2F promoters bind repressive PRC1.6/E2F6 complexes.
source: Proteomic and biochemical experiments demonstrate the binding of wildtype but not mutant E2F promoters by repressive PRC1.6/E2F6 and DREAM/E2F4 complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through SILAC proteomics and ChIP experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Wildtype E2F promoters bind repressive DREAM/E2F4 complexes.
source: Proteomic and biochemical experiments demonstrate the binding of wildtype but not mutant E2F promoters by repressive PRC1.6/E2F6 and DREAM/E2F4 complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through SILAC proteomics and ChIP experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Mutant E2F promoters do not bind repressive PRC1.6/E2F6 complexes.
source: Proteomic and biochemical experiments demonstrate the binding of wildtype but not mutant E2F promoters by repressive PRC1.6/E2F6 and DREAM/E2F4 complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through SILAC proteomics experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutant E2F promoters do not bind repressive DREAM/E2F4 complexes.
source: Proteomic and biochemical experiments demonstrate the binding of wildtype but not mutant E2F promoters by repressive PRC1.6/E2F6 and DREAM/E2F4 complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through SILAC proteomics experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Knockdown studies confirm the involvement of repressive E2F complexes in regulating A3B expression.
source: Knockdown and overexpression studies confirm the involvement of these repressive complexes in regulating A3B expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression studies confirm the involvement of repressive E2F complexes in regulating A3B expression.
source: Knockdown and overexpression studies confirm the involvement of these repressive complexes in regulating A3B expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated through E2F overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A3B expression is suppressed in normal cells by repressive E2F complexes.
source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that A3B expression is suppressed in normal cells by repressive E2F complexes and that viral or mutational disruption of this regulatory network triggers overexpression in breast cancer and provides fuel for tumor evolution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Viral disruption of the E2F regulatory network triggers A3B overexpression in breast cancer.
source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that A3B expression is suppressed in normal cells by repressive E2F complexes and that viral or mutational disruption of this regulatory network triggers overexpression in breast cancer and provides fuel for tumor evolution.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with polyomavirus T antigen and literature on HPV.

claim: Mutational disruption of the E2F regulatory network triggers A3B overexpression in breast cancer.
source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that A3B expression is suppressed in normal cells by repressive E2F complexes and that viral or mutational disruption of this regulatory network triggers overexpression in breast cancer and provides fuel for tumor evolution.
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR/Cas9 experiments and TCGA data analyses.

claim: A3B overexpression provides fuel for tumor evolution.
source: Altogether, these studies demonstrate that A3B expression is suppressed in normal cells by repressive E2F complexes and that viral or mutational disruption of this regulatory network triggers overexpression in breast cancer and provides fuel for tumor evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenic activity of A3B and supported by TCGA analyses showing associations with APOBEC mutation signatures.

claim: APOBEC mutation signatures consist of C-to-T transitions and C-to-G transversions occurring at cytosine nucleobases in 5'-TCW motifs.
source: The APOBEC mutation signature consists of C-to-T transitions and C-to-G transversions occurring at cytosine nucleobases in 5'-TCW motifs (W = A or T; SBS2 and SBS13), respectively (Alexandrov et al., 2020; Alexandrov et al., 2013; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The human APOBEC family has nine active family members: APOBEC1, AID, and APOBEC3A/B/C/D/F/G/H.
source: The human APOBEC family has nine active family members: APOBEC1, AID, and APOBEC3A/B/C/D/F/G/H (reviewed by Green and Weitzman, 2019; Harris and Dudley, 2015; Ito et al., 2020; Olson et al., 2018; Silvas and Schiffer, 2019; Simon et al., 2015; Siriwardena et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited reviews.

claim: A3B is overexpressed in a large fraction of tumors.
source: First, A3B is overexpressed in a large fraction of tumors (Burns et al., 2013a; Burns et al., 2013b; Ng et al., 2019; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A3B is the only deaminase family member localizing to the nuclear compartment.
source: Second, A3B is the only deaminase family member localizing to the nuclear compartment (Bogerd et al., 2006; Burns et al., 2013a; Lackey et al., 2012; Lackey et al., 2013; Pak et al., 2011; Salamango et al., 2018; Stenglein et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A3B overexpression triggers strong DNA damage responses and overt cytotoxicity.
source: Third, A3B overexpression triggers strong DNA damage responses and overt cytotoxicity (Burns et al., 2013a; Nikkilä et al., 2017; Serebrenik et al., 2019; Taylor et al., 2013; Yamazaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A3B expression correlates positively with APOBEC signature mutation loads in breast cancer.
source: Fourth, A3B expression correlates positively with APOBEC signature mutation loads in breast cancer (Burns et al., 2013a), and its overexpression associates with branched evolution in breast and lung cancer (de Bruin et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2019; Roper et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A3B overexpression associates with branched evolution in breast and lung cancer.
source: Fourth, A3B expression correlates positively with APOBEC signature mutation loads in breast cancer (Burns et al., 2013a), and its overexpression associates with branched evolution in breast and lung cancer (de Bruin et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2019; Roper et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A3B expression is induced by human papillomavirus (HPV) infections.
source: Fifth, A3B expression is induced by human papillomavirus (HPV) and polyomavirus (PyV) infections, which relates to the fact that cervical, head/neck, and bladder cancers have high proportions of APOBEC signature mutations (Gillison et al., 2019; Henderson et al., 2014; Starrett et al., 2019; Verhalen et al., 2016; Vieira et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A3B expression is induced by polyomavirus (PyV) infections.
source: Fifth, A3B expression is induced by human papillomavirus (HPV) and polyomavirus (PyV) infections, which relates to the fact that cervical, head/neck, and bladder cancers have high proportions of APOBEC signature mutations (Gillison et al., 2019; Henderson et al., 2014; Starrett et al., 2019; Verhalen et al., 2016; Vieira et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Cervical, head/neck, and bladder cancers have high proportions of APOBEC signature mutations.
source: Fifth, A3B expression is induced by human papillomavirus (HPV) and polyomavirus (PyV) infections, which relates to the fact that cervical, head/neck, and bladder cancers have high proportions of APOBEC signature mutations (Gillison et al., 2019; Henderson et al., 2014; Starrett et al., 2019; Verhalen et al., 2016; Vieira et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: A3B overexpression associates with poor clinical outcomes including drug resistance and metastasis.
source: Last, A3B overexpression associates with poor clinical outcomes including drug resistance and metastasis (Glaser et al., 2018; Law et al., 2016; Serebrenik et al., 2020; Sieuwerts et al., 2017; Sieuwerts et al., 2014; Walker et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015; Yamazaki et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: In a subset of cancer types, A3B exerts genotoxic stress that sensitizes tumor cells to DNA damaging chemotherapies.
source: However, in a different subset of cancer types, A3B has been shown to exert genotoxic stress that sensitizes tumor cells to DNA damaging chemotherapies (Glaser et al., 2018; Serebrenik et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Phorbol myristic acid (PMA) induces A3B by activating the protein kinase C (PKC) signal transduction pathway.
source: Phorbol myristic acid (PMA) and lymphotoxin-β induce A3B by activating the protein kinase C (PKC) and non-canonical (nc)NF-κB signal transduction pathways (Leonard et al., 2015; Lucifora et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Lymphotoxin-β induces A3B by activating the non-canonical (nc)NF-κB signal transduction pathway.
source: Phorbol myristic acid (PMA) and lymphotoxin-β induce A3B by activating the protein kinase C (PKC) and non-canonical (nc)NF-κB signal transduction pathways (Leonard et al., 2015; Lucifora et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Canonical NF-κB activation leads to A3B upregulation.
source: Canonical NF-κB activation also leads to A3B upregulation (Maruyama et al., 2016) suggesting a mechanistic linkage between inflammatory responses and cancer mutagenesis.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Various DNA damaging agents stimulate A3B expression including hydroxyurea, gemcitabine, aphidicolin, and camptothecin.
source: Various DNA damaging agents also stimulate A3B expression including hydroxyurea, gemcitabine, aphidicolin, and camptothecin (Kanu et al., 2016; Yamazaki et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: HPV infection induces A3B expression by mechanisms requiring the viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins.
source: Interestingly, as alluded above, HPV infection induces A3B expression by mechanisms requiring the viral E6 and E7 oncoproteins (Mori et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2017; Starrett et al., 2019; Verhalen et al., 2016; Vieira et al., 2014; Warren et al., 2015; Westrich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: HPV E6 induces A3B in part by recruiting the transcription factor TEAD4 to promoter sequences.
source: E6 appears to induce A3B in part by recruiting the transcription factor TEAD4 to promoter sequences (Mori et al., 2015; Mori et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: JC and BK PyV upregulate A3B transcription by a mechanism requiring the LxCxE motif of the viral large T antigen.
source: JC and BK PyV upregulate A3B transcription by a mechanism requiring the LxCxE motif of the viral large T antigen (TAg; Starrett et al., 2019; Verhalen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: HPV E7 has a LxCxE motif.
source: HPV E7 also has a LxCxE motif suggesting a shared mechanism in which these viral oncoproteins may activate A3B transcription by antagonizing the canonical retinoblastoma tumor suppressor protein RB1 and the related pocket proteins RB-like 1 (RBL1) and RBL2 (reviewed by An et al., 2012; Bellacchio and Paggi, 2013; DeCaprio, 2014; DeCaprio and Garcea, 2013; Rashid et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited reviews.

claim: The RB/E2F axis is frequently disrupted in non-viral cancers such as breast cancer, HPV-negative head/neck cancer, and lung cancer.
source: The RB/E2F axis is also frequently disrupted in non-viral cancers such as breast cancer, HPV-negative head/neck cancer, and lung cancer (Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012; Ertel et al., 2010; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited TCGA studies.

claim: E2F1, E2F2, and E2F3 bind target promoters and recruit additional activating proteins to stimulate the expression of cell cycle genes during G1/S.
source: E2F1, E2F2, and E2F3 bind target promoters and recruit additional activating proteins to stimulate the expression of cell cycle genes during G1/S.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E2F function.

claim: RB1 binds the transactivation domain of E2F1, E2F2, and E2F3 and thereby prevents the recruitment of transcription activating factors.
source: RB1 binds the transactivation domain of these E2Fs and thereby prevents the recruitment of transcription activating factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RB1 function.

claim: E2F4 and E2F5 form complexes with RBL1 or RBL2 and further associate with the MuvB complex.
source: E2F4 and E2F5 form complexes with RBL1 or RBL2 and further associate with the MuvB complex, which includes LIN9, LIN37, LIN52, LIN54, and RBBP4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DREAM complex composition.

claim: The MuvB complex includes LIN9, LIN37, LIN52, LIN54, and RBBP4.
source: E2F4 and E2F5 form complexes with RBL1 or RBL2 and further associate with the MuvB complex, which includes LIN9, LIN37, LIN52, LIN54, and RBBP4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MuvB complex composition.

claim: The DREAM complex represses transcription during the G0 and early G1 phases of the cell cycle.
source: This bipartite assembly, known as the DREAM complex, represses transcription during the G0 and early G1 phases of the cell cycle (Litovchick et al., 2011; Litovchick et al., 2007; Pilkinton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Endogenous Cyclin/CDK complexes dissociate RBL1 and RBL2 from E2F4 and E2F5 and thereby activate transcription.
source: Endogenous Cyclin/CDK complexes, as well as HPV E7 and PyV TAg through LxCxE motifs, dissociate RBL1 and RBL2 from E2F4 and E2F5 and thereby activate transcription (reviewed by An et al., 2012; Bellacchio and Paggi, 2013; DeCaprio, 2014; DeCaprio and Garcea, 2013; Rashid et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited reviews.

claim: HPV E7 and PyV TAg dissociate RBL1 and RBL2 from E2F4 and E2F5 through LxCxE motifs and thereby activate transcription.
source: Endogenous Cyclin/CDK complexes, as well as HPV E7 and PyV TAg through LxCxE motifs, dissociate RBL1 and RBL2 from E2F4 and E2F5 and thereby activate transcription (reviewed by An et al., 2012; Bellacchio and Paggi, 2013; DeCaprio, 2014; DeCaprio and Garcea, 2013; Rashid et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited reviews.

claim: E2F6, E2F7, and E2F8 exert their repressive function independent of RB1, RBL1, and RBL2.
source: E2F6, E2F7, and E2F8 exert their repressive function independent of RB1, RBL1, and RBL2 (Christensen et al., 2005; de Bruin et al., 2003; Trimarchi et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: E2F6 functions in the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC)1.6 complex to repress gene expression during G1-S.
source: E2F6 functions in the Polycomb Repressive Complex (PRC)1.6 complex to repress gene expression during G1-S (Qin et al., 2012; Scelfo et al., 2019; Stielow et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The PRC1.6 complex consists of MGA, L3MBTL2, PCGF6, WDR5, E2F6, and TFDP1 (among other proteins).
source: The PRC1.6 complex consists of MGA, L3MBTL2, PCGF6, WDR5, E2F6, and TFDP1 (among other proteins), and directly binds DNA through MGA, L3MBTL2, and E2F6 (Stielow et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The PRC1.6 complex directly binds DNA through MGA, L3MBTL2, and E2F6.
source: The PRC1.6 complex consists of MGA, L3MBTL2, PCGF6, WDR5, E2F6, and TFDP1 (among other proteins), and directly binds DNA through MGA, L3MBTL2, and E2F6 (Stielow et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: E2F7 and E2F8 repress genes through the S-phase and prevent gene reactivation during the next cell cycle.
source: Finally, E2F7 and E2F8 repress genes through the S-phase and prevent gene reactivation during the next cell cycle (Cuitiño et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: A3B expression is low in normal tissues.
source: Our previous studies showed that A3B expression is low in normal tissues (Burns et al., 2013a; Refsland et al., 2010) and inducible upon PyV TAg expression (Starrett et al., 2019; Verhalen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: A3B expression is inducible upon PyV TAg expression.
source: Our previous studies showed that A3B expression is low in normal tissues (Burns et al., 2013a; Refsland et al., 2010) and inducible upon PyV TAg expression (Starrett et al., 2019; Verhalen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature from the authors' previous work.

claim: The A3B-luciferase reporter construct contains a 950 bp region spanning the A3B transcription start site (−900 to +50 relative to the +1 of the A3B TSS).
source: To study the mechanism of A3B transcriptional regulation, a 950 bp region spanning the A3B transcription start site (TSS) was cloned upstream of a firefly luciferase reporter (i.e. −900 to +50 relative to the +1 of the A3B TSS; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the construction of the reporter used in the study.

claim: In MCF10A and MCF7 cells, the A3B-luciferase construct supports modest levels of transcription activity above those of a promoter-less vector.
source: In MCF10A normal-like breast epithelial cells and MCF7 breast cancer cells, which both express low levels of A3B (Burns et al., 2013a), this construct supported modest levels of transcription activity above those of a promoter-less vector (compare black bars of pGL3-basic versus pA3B-luciferase in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MCF10A and MCF7 cells both express low levels of A3B.
source: In MCF10A normal-like breast epithelial cells and MCF7 breast cancer cells, which both express low levels of A3B (Burns et al., 2013a), this construct supported modest levels of transcription activity above those of a promoter-less vector (compare black bars of pGL3-basic versus pA3B-luciferase in Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Transcription of the A3B-luciferase reporter is induced strongly in cells co-expressing the BK PyV truncated T antigen (tTAg).
source: Interestingly, similar to upregulation of the endogenous A3B gene in our previous studies (Starrett et al., 2019), transcription of the A3B-luciferase reporter was induced strongly in cells co-expressing the BK PyV truncated T antigen (tTAg) but not in cells co-expressing a LxCxE mutant tTAg (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Transcription of the A3B-luciferase reporter is not induced in cells co-expressing a LxCxE mutant tTAg.
source: Interestingly, similar to upregulation of the endogenous A3B gene in our previous studies (Starrett et al., 2019), transcription of the A3B-luciferase reporter was induced strongly in cells co-expressing the BK PyV truncated T antigen (tTAg) but not in cells co-expressing a LxCxE mutant tTAg (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The JASPAR database predicted five putative E2F binding sites within the −900 to +50 A3B promoter region.
source: The JASPAR database (Fornes et al., 2020) was then used to predict transcription factor binding sites within the −900 to +50 A3B promoter region. This analysis yielded dozens of candidate sites including five putative E2F binding sites (labeled A-E in Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics analysis performed.

claim: Clustered base substitution mutations in E2F sites A, B, and C had negligible effects on basal or tTAg-induced levels of luciferase reporter expression.
source: Clustered base substitution mutations in sites A, B, and C had negligible effects on basal or tTAg-induced levels of luciferase reporter expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Clustered mutations in E2F site D caused a two- to three-fold reduction in both basal and tTAg-induced levels of luciferase reporter expression.
source: Clustered mutations in site D caused a two- to three-fold reduction in both basal and tTAg-induced levels of luciferase reporter expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Clustered mutations in E2F site E caused a strong five-fold induction of A3B-luciferase reporter activity that could not be further increased by tTAg co-expression.
source: However, clustered mutations in site E, located at +21 to +28 relative to the TSS, caused a strong five-fold induction of A3B-luciferase reporter activity that could not be further increased by tTAg co-expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: E2F site E is located at +21 to +28 relative to the TSS.
source: However, clustered mutations in site E, located at +21 to +28 relative to the TSS, caused a strong five-fold induction of A3B-luciferase reporter activity that could not be further increased by tTAg co-expression.
evidence: This describes the location of E2F site E.

claim: Mutations in E2F site E were epistatic to those in site D.
source: Mutations in site E were also epistatic to those in site D, suggesting that site E may be the dominant regulatory site.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 1.

claim: E2F site E may be the dominant regulatory site.
source: Mutations in site E were also epistatic to those in site D, suggesting that site E may be the dominant regulatory site.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis data.

claim: The +12 to +30 region of the A3B promoter including site E is normally bound by a repressive factor.
source: Taken together, these results suggested that the +12 to +30 region of the A3B promoter including site E is normally bound by a repressive factor and different mutations prevent repression and allow high levels of transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data.

claim: 114 genes have expression profiles positively associating with A3B (Spearman's rho ≥0.5) in TCGA breast cancer RNA-seq data sets.
source: To gain additional insights into the possible involvement of an E2F complex in A3B transcriptional repression, TCGA breast cancer RNA-seq data sets were used to identify 114 genes with expression profiles positively associating with A3B (Spearman's rho ≥0.5; n = 1,097 RNA-seq data sets; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics analysis performed on TCGA data.

claim: 87% of genes positively associating with A3B were shown to be bound by repressive E2F complexes.
source: Remarkably, 87% of these genes were shown to be bound by repressive E2F complexes suggesting a common regulatory mechanism (Litovchick et al., 2007; Müller et al., 2014; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published E2F target gene lists.

claim: A3B mRNA levels across primary breast cancer associate strongly with expression levels of MELK and FOXM1.
source: For instance, A3B mRNA levels across primary breast cancer associated strongly with expression levels of MELK and FOXM1 (Figure 2A), which both have well-described E2F-dependent repression mechanisms (Litovchick et al., 2007; Müller et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2014; Verlinden et al., 2005).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the heatmap in Figure 2A.

claim: MELK and FOXM1 both have well-described E2F-dependent repression mechanisms.
source: For instance, A3B mRNA levels across primary breast cancer associated strongly with expression levels of MELK and FOXM1 (Figure 2A), which both have well-described E2F-dependent repression mechanisms (Litovchick et al., 2007; Müller et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2014; Verlinden et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: A subset of coordinately expressed genes has a predicted consensus (or near-consensus) cell cycle gene homology region (CHR) element adjacent to the predicted E2F binding site.
source: A subset of these coordinately expressed genes also has a predicted consensus (or near-consensus) cell cycle gene homology region (CHR) element adjacent to the predicted E2F binding site (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Juxtaposed CHR and E2F elements cooperatively facilitate the binding of repressive E2F complexes and suppress gene expression.
source: When juxtaposed, these two elements cooperatively facilitate the binding of repressive E2F complexes and suppress gene expression (Müller et al., 2012; Müller et al., 2017; Müller et al., 2014) and reviewed by Fischer and Müller, 2017; Sadasivam and DeCaprio, 2013.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: In the A3B promoter, both the predicted CHR (+9 to +14) and E2F (+21 to +28) elements occur within the +12 to +30 region.
source: Interestingly, in the A3B promoter, both the predicted CHR (+9 to +14) and E2F (+21 to +28) elements occur within the +12 to +30 region defined above in mutagenesis experiments (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This connects the bioinformatics predictions with the mutagenesis data.

claim: The global profile of A3B mRNA expression in primary breast cancer is distinct from related A3 genes except for A3A.
source: The global profile of A3B mRNA expression in primary breast cancer is distinct from related A3 genes except for A3A (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in the heatmap in Figure 2A.

claim: Differences in CHR and E2F sites in individual A3 gene promoters explain the distinct expression profiles.
source: This is explained by differences at potentially critical nucleobase positions in both the CHR and E2F sites in the individual A3 gene promoters including the most closely related A3C promoter region (Figure 2C and see below).
evidence: This is inferred from sequence comparisons shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The A3B promoter region including juxtaposed CHR and E2F elements is conserved in hominids and Old World monkeys.
source: Sequence comparisons with other primates demonstrate that this region of the A3B promoter, including juxtaposed CHR and E2F elements, is conserved in hominids and Old World monkeys (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence alignments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Adjacent CHR and E2F sites in the A3B promoter are unique amongst A3 genes.
source: Thus, adjacent CHR and E2F sites in the A3B promoter are unique amongst A3 genes, specific to humans and other higher primates, and likely linked to the aforementioned expression patterns.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence comparisons.

claim: Adjacent CHR and E2F sites in the A3B promoter are specific to humans and other higher primates.
source: Thus, adjacent CHR and E2F sites in the A3B promoter are unique amongst A3 genes, specific to humans and other higher primates, and likely linked to the aforementioned expression patterns.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Altering the nucleobase immediately 5' of the predicted E2F binding site (+20 A-to-T) had no effect on reporter activity.
source: Altering the nucleobase immediately 5' of the predicted E2F binding site (+20 A-to-T) had no effect, and changing the first nucleobase of the predicted E2F binding site (+21 G-to-C) caused slight reporter activation but did not affect tTAg inducibility (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Changing the first nucleobase of the predicted E2F binding site (+21 G-to-C) caused slight reporter activation but did not affect tTAg inducibility.
source: Altering the nucleobase immediately 5' of the predicted E2F binding site (+20 A-to-T) had no effect, and changing the first nucleobase of the predicted E2F binding site (+21 G-to-C) caused slight reporter activation but did not affect tTAg inducibility (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Single nucleobase changes in the core of the predicted E2F binding site (+22 C-to-G or +23 G-to-C) caused full de-repression of the A3B-luciferase reporter that could not be further increased by tTAg.
source: In contrast, single nucleobase changes in the core of the predicted E2F binding site (+22 C-to-G or +23 G-to-C) caused full de-repression of the A3B-luciferase reporter that could not be further increased by tTAg (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Single and combinatorial base substitution mutations in the CHR element resulted in partial or full de-repression of the A3B-luciferase reporter.
source: Single and combinatorial base substitution mutations in the CHR element also resulted in partial or full de-repression of the A3B-luciferase reporter (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mutation of +10 TC-to-CT in the CHR element caused partial reporter de-repression, which could still be further enhanced by tTAg.
source: For instance, mutation of +10 TC-to-CT or +9 TT-to-AA caused partial reporter de-repression, which could still be further enhanced by tTAg.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mutation of +9 TT-to-AA in the CHR element caused partial reporter de-repression, which could still be further enhanced by tTAg.
source: For instance, mutation of +10 TC-to-CT or +9 TT-to-AA caused partial reporter de-repression, which could still be further enhanced by tTAg.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mutating the two adenine nucleobases at the 3' end of the CHR element (+13 AA-to-TT) resulted in full reporter de-repression which could not be increased by tTAg.
source: In contrast, mutating the two adenine nucleobases at the 3' end of the CHR element (+13 AA-to-TT) resulted in full reporter de-repression which could not be increased by tTAg.
evidence: This is demonstrated by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Both the putative E2F binding site and the adjacent CHR element are essential for repressing A3B transcription.
source: These fine-mapping results showed that both the putative E2F binding site and the adjacent CHR element are essential for repressing A3B transcription.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis data in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Four independent CRISPR/Cas9-targeted clones showed elevated A3B protein levels in comparison to control lacZ clones.
source: Four independent targeted clones showed elevated A3B protein levels in comparison to control lacZ clones, consistent with a repressive function for the putative E2F binding site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Seven independent HDR clones with tandem base substitution mutations C22G and G25C showed robust increases in both A3B protein and mRNA levels.
source: Seven independent clones were obtained with the desired two base substitution mutations (Figure 3B). All seven showed robust increases in both A3B protein and mRNA levels with differences potentially due to clonal variation (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The mRNA levels of related A3 family members were unaffected by targeted genomic changes in the A3B promoter.
source: The mRNA levels of related A3 family members were unaffected, which further confirmed specificity of the targeted genomic changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The endogenous E2F site at base pairs +21 to +28 of the A3B promoter contributes to transcriptional repression in MCF10A cells.
source: These results demonstrated that the endogenous E2F site at base pairs +21 to +28 of the A3B promoter contributes to transcriptional repression in MCF10A cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the HDR experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: tTAg had no effect on A3B mRNA or protein levels in HDR targeted MCF10A clones.
source: Importantly, tTAg had no effect on A3B mRNA or protein levels in the HDR targeted MCF10A clones (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: All of the observed A3B induction by tTAg is mediated by the single endogenous E2F site.
source: Nevertheless, these results combined to demonstrate that all of the observed A3B induction by tTAg is mediated by this single endogenous E2F site.
evidence: This is concluded from the tTAg experiments with HDR clones shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PMA caused similar induction of A3B mRNA and protein levels from both the wildtype endogenous promoter and the HDR-engineered promoter with tandem base substitution mutations C22G and G25C.
source: Interestingly, PMA caused similar induction of A3B mRNA and protein levels from both the wildtype endogenous promoter (lacZ controls) as well as the HDR-engineered promoter with tandem base substitution mutations C22G and G25C (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RT-qPCR and immunoblot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Simultaneous de-repression through HDR-targeted mutation of the single E2F site and activation by PMA caused a thirty-fold increase in A3B levels above the uninduced basal level.
source: Overall, simultaneous de-repression through HDR-targeted mutation of the single E2F site and activation by PMA caused a thirty-fold increase in A3B levels above the uninduced basal level in the lacZ controls.
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A3B expression is impacted independently by tTAg/E2F and PKC/ncNF-κB signal transduction mechanisms.
source: Together with the above data above, these results demonstrated that A3B expression is impacted independently by tTAg/E2F and PKC/ncNF-κB and signal transduction mechanisms.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined tTAg and PMA experiments shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: In an experiment comparing proteins bound to the wildtype A3B promoter sequence versus a promoter sequence with mutations spanning the predicted E2F binding site, a greater than four-fold enrichment was observed for almost all proteins in the repressive DREAM complex.
source: Interestingly, in an experiment comparing proteins bound to the wildtype A3B promoter sequence versus a promoter sequence with mutations spanning the predicted E2F binding site (matching the +22-to-30 mutant in Figure 1D–E), a greater than four-fold enrichment was observed for almost all proteins in the repressive DREAM complex, including TFDP1, TFDP2, RBL1, RBL2, E2F4, E2F5, and the MuvB components LIN9, LIN37, LIN52, and LIN54 (Figure 4B–C and Supplementary file 2; confirmatory immunoblots for representative enriched proteins in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Most members of the DREAM complex preferentially bound to the wildtype but not to the A3B mutant promoter sequence with a single-base substitution +22 C-to-G.
source: Given that a single-base substitution +22 C-to-G was sufficient for full de-repression in reporter assays (Figure 2E), we repeated the SILAC DNA pull-downs comparing the wildtype promoter sequence and this mutant. Importantly, again, most members of the DREAM complex preferentially bound to the wildtype but not to the A3B mutant promoter sequence (Figure 4B,D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: DREAM complex components were enriched in a proteomics experiment comparing MCF7 nuclear proteins bound to the wildtype A3B promoter versus a promoter sequence with mutations spanning the CHR element.
source: Similar enrichments for DREAM complex components were also evident in a separate proteomics experiment comparing MCF7 nuclear proteins bound to the wildtype A3B promoter versus a promoter sequence with mutations spanning the CHR element (matching the +12-to-20 mutant in Figure 1D–E; Figure 4B, E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 4B,E.

claim: The CHR site is required for A3B promoter binding by the DREAM complex.
source: These additional results indicated that the CHR site is also required for A3B promoter binding by the DREAM complex and that the E2F site alone is insufficient.
evidence: This is concluded from the proteomics data comparing wildtype and CHR mutant promoters.

claim: The E2F site alone is insufficient for A3B promoter binding by the DREAM complex.
source: These additional results indicated that the CHR site is also required for A3B promoter binding by the DREAM complex and that the E2F site alone is insufficient.
evidence: This is concluded from the proteomics data.

claim: Components of the PRC1.6 complex (E2F6, MGA, and L3MTBL2) were found enriched in binding to wildtype but not to E2F or CHR mutant A3B promoter sequences.
source: Interestingly, the proteomics data sets also implicated components of the PRC1.6 complex in binding to wildtype but not to E2F or CHR mutant A3B promoter sequences. In particular, E2F6, MGA, and L3MTBL2 were found enriched repeatedly (Figure 4B–E, Supplementary file 2, and confirmatory immunoblots for representative enriched proteins in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SILAC proteomics data shown in Figure 4B-E.

claim: Two additional PRC1.6 components, PCGF6 and WDR5, approached the four-fold cut-off in one dataset.
source: Two additional PRC1.6 components, PCGF6 and WDR5, also approached the four-fold cut-off in one dataset (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is shown in the supplementary data.

claim: The repressive PRC1.6 complex is capable of binding to the wildtype A3B promoter sequence.
source: These results indicated that the repressive PRC1.6 complex is also capable of binding to the wildtype A3B promoter sequence and may therefore also play a role in suppressing expression.
evidence: This is concluded from the proteomics data.

claim: The wildtype A3B promoter in lacZ4 cells showed similarly strong enrichment for binding by both E2F4 and E2F6.
source: The wildtype A3B promoter in lacZ4 cells showed similarly strong enrichment for binding by both E2F4 and E2F6, and single-base substitutions in E2F site E in HDR49 cells reduced binding of both proteins to background levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Single-base substitutions in E2F site E in HDR49 cells reduced binding of both E2F4 and E2F6 to background levels.
source: The wildtype A3B promoter in lacZ4 cells showed similarly strong enrichment for binding by both E2F4 and E2F6, and single-base substitutions in E2F site E in HDR49 cells reduced binding of both proteins to background levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Significant E2F4 enrichment was evident in the promoter regions of RAD51 and TTK.
source: In parallel analyses, significant E2F4 enrichment was evident in the promoter regions of two established E2F4/DREAM-repressed genes, RAD51 and TTK (Dean et al., 2012; Engeland, 2018; Müller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: E2F6 was enriched only at the RAD51 promoter and not the TTK promoter.
source: E2F6 was enriched only at the RAD51 promoter and not the TTK promoter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: L3MBTL2 showed strong binding to the A3B promoter, intermediate levels to the RAD51 promoter, and insignificant levels to the TTK promoter.
source: ChIP experiments for L3MBTL2 revealed strong binding of this PRC1.6 component to the A3B promoter, intermediate levels to the RAD51 promoter, and insignificant levels to the TTK promoter (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The A3B promoter can be occupied by both E2F4 and E2F6 complexes.
source: These ChIP experiments indicated that the A3B promoter can be occupied by both E2F4 and E2F6 complexes, that the binding of either complex requires an intact +21 to +28 E2F site, and that the binding of the same proteins to other established E2F sites can vary significantly within the same cell population.
evidence: This is concluded from the ChIP data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The binding of E2F4 and E2F6 complexes to the A3B promoter requires an intact +21 to +28 E2F site.
source: These ChIP experiments indicated that the A3B promoter can be occupied by both E2F4 and E2F6 complexes, that the binding of either complex requires an intact +21 to +28 E2F site, and that the binding of the same proteins to other established E2F sites can vary significantly within the same cell population.
evidence: This is concluded from the ChIP data comparing lacZ4 and HDR49 cells shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The binding of E2F4 and E2F6 to other established E2F sites can vary significantly within the same cell population.
source: These ChIP experiments indicated that the A3B promoter can be occupied by both E2F4 and E2F6 complexes, that the binding of either complex requires an intact +21 to +28 E2F site, and that the binding of the same proteins to other established E2F sites can vary significantly within the same cell population.
evidence: This is concluded from the ChIP data comparing A3B, RAD51, and TTK promoters shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: E2F4 depletion alone did not alter A3B expression in MCF10A cells.
source: Surprisingly, E2F4 depletion alone did not alter A3B expression, whereas E2F6 depletion caused an increase in A3B protein levels by immunoblotting (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: E2F6 depletion caused an increase in A3B protein levels in MCF10A cells.
source: Surprisingly, E2F4 depletion alone did not alter A3B expression, whereas E2F6 depletion caused an increase in A3B protein levels by immunoblotting (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Combined E2F4/E2F6 depletion increases A3B protein levels more than E2F6 alone.
source: We also observed that combined E2F4/E2F6 depletion increases A3B protein levels more than E2F6 alone, indicating that both complexes contribute to repression with the latter potentially being more dominant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Both E2F4 and E2F6 complexes contribute to A3B repression with E2F6 potentially being more dominant.
source: We also observed that combined E2F4/E2F6 depletion increases A3B protein levels more than E2F6 alone, indicating that both complexes contribute to repression with the latter potentially being more dominant.
evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression of either E2F4 or E2F6, as well as E2F5, was able to repress A3B expression to varying extents in multiple different breast cancer cell lines.
source: Conversely, overexpression of either E2F4 or E2F6, as well as E2F5 which also forms a DREAM complex (Litovchick et al., 2007), was able to repress A3B expression to varying extents in multiple different breast cancer cell lines (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Both E2F4/DREAM and E2F6/PRC1.6 complexes can occupy the A3B promoter and repress transcription.
source: Taken together, the ChIP, knockdown, and overexpression studies indicate that both E2F4/DREAM and E2F6/PRC1.6 complexes can occupy the A3B promoter and repress transcription.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined ChIP, knockdown, and overexpression data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The PRC1.6 complex repression mechanism may predominate over the DREAM complex in A3B regulation.
source: Moreover, the significant A3B upregulation observed upon E2F6 knockdown but not E2F4 knockdown suggests that the PRC1.6 complex repression mechanism may predominate.
evidence: This is inferred from the knockdown data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Breast tumors frequently display A3B overexpression and APOBEC signature mutations.
source: Breast tumors frequently display A3B overexpression and APOBEC signature mutations (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Angus et al., 2019; Bertucci et al., 2019; Burns et al., 2013a; Burns et al., 2013b; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Association studies with large breast cancer cohorts have shown only weak positive or negligible associations between A3B expression levels and APOBEC signature mutation loads.
source: However, association studies with large breast cancer cohorts have shown only weak positive or negligible associations between A3B expression levels and APOBEC signature mutation loads, and clear outliers exist including tumors with high A3B and few APOBEC signature mutations and low A3B and many APOBEC signature mutations (Buisson et al., 2019; Burns et al., 2013a; Burns et al., 2013b; Nik-Zainal et al., 2014; Roberts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Tumors with common high-expressing genes showed an average of twenty-fold higher A3B mRNA levels than tumors with common low-expressing genes.
source: As expected from the analysis work-flow and the likelihood of a shared transcriptional regulation mechanism, tumors with common high-expressing genes showed an average of twenty-fold higher A3B mRNA levels than tumors with common low-expressing genes (p<2.4×10−6 by Welch's test; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tumors with the common high-expressing genes showed an average of 9.3% APOBEC signature mutations versus 3.2% in the common low group.
source: More interestingly, tumors with the common high-expressing genes showed an average of 9.3% APOBEC signature mutations versus 3.2% in the common low group (p=0.026 by Welch's test; Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Significantly higher APOBEC mutation signature enrichment values were evident in tumors defined by the common set of high-expressed genes in comparison to tumors with the same genes expressed at low levels.
source: As an independent metric, significantly higher APOBEC mutation signature enrichment values were evident in tumors defined by the common set of high-expressed genes in comparison to tumors with the same genes expressed at low levels (p=0.003 by Welch's test; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Coordinated overexpression of an RB/E2F-repressed gene set may be a better indicator for APOBEC mutation susceptibility than expression of A3B itself.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that coordinated overexpression of an RB/E2F-repressed gene set may be a better indicator for APOBEC mutation susceptibility than expression of A3B itself.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the analyses in Figure 6A-D versus Figure 6E-H.

claim: E2F4/DREAM and E2F6/PRC1.6 complexes combine to repress A3B transcription.
source: Our results support a model in which E2F4/DREAM and E2F6/PRC1.6 complexes combine to repress A3B transcription (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main model proposed based on all the experimental data.

claim: These two complexes are likely to compete for binding to the same conserved E2F site located at +21 to +28 of the A3B promoter.
source: These two complexes are likely to compete for binding to the same conserved E2F site located at +21 to +28 of the A3B promoter because tandem base substitution mutations (C22G and G25C) de-repress expression of endogenous A3B and render the locus non-responsive to further activation by tTAg (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is inferred from the HDR experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The E2F-governed regulatory mechanism provides an attractive explanation for a large proportion of reported A3B overexpression in both viral and non-viral cancer types.
source: The E2F-governed regulatory mechanism described here provides an attractive explanation for a large proportion of reported A3B overexpression in both viral and non-viral cancer types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and literature context.

claim: The HPV E7 and PyV TAg oncoproteins may trigger A3B upregulation directly by dissociating repressive E2F complexes.
source: For instance, the HPV E7 and PyV TAg oncoproteins may trigger A3B upregulation directly by dissociating repressive E2F complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the study's findings and established knowledge about viral oncoproteins.

claim: Cervical cancers are almost invariably HPV-positive, A3B-overexpressing, and enriched for APOBEC signature mutations.
source: Accordingly, cervical cancers are almost invariably HPV-positive, A3B-overexpressing, and enriched for APOBEC signature mutations (Burns et al., 2013b; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017; Roberts et al., 2013; Zapatka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: HPV-positive head/neck cancers show A3B-overexpression and APOBEC mutation signature enrichment.
source: HPV-positive head/neck cancers also show A3B-overexpression and APOBEC mutation signature enrichment (Burns et al., 2013b; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Cannataro et al., 2019; Faden et al., 2017; Roberts et al., 2013; Vieira et al., 2014; Zapatka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Many HPV-negative cancers elicit similarly high A3B expression levels and APOBEC mutation burdens.
source: Importantly, many HPV-negative cancers elicit similarly high A3B expression levels and APOBEC mutation burdens (Burns et al., 2013b; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Cannataro et al., 2019; Gillison et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: HPV status in head/neck cancer appears mutually exclusive with alterations of RB/E2F axis genes.
source: Moreover, HPV status in head/neck cancer appears mutually exclusive with alterations of RB/E2F axis genes, such that HPV-negative cancers often display copy number loss of CDKN2A (encoding p16) and overexpression of CCND1 (encoding Cyclin D1; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Gillison et al., 2019; Zapatka et al., 2020), which effectively mimics a subset of the oncogenic effects of E7.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: HPV-negative head/neck cancers often display copy number loss of CDKN2A (encoding p16) and overexpression of CCND1 (encoding Cyclin D1).
source: Moreover, HPV status in head/neck cancer appears mutually exclusive with alterations of RB/E2F axis genes, such that HPV-negative cancers often display copy number loss of CDKN2A (encoding p16) and overexpression of CCND1 (encoding Cyclin D1; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Gillison et al., 2019; Zapatka et al., 2020), which effectively mimics a subset of the oncogenic effects of E7.
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: Both virus-dependent and independent tumors may exploit the same pathway to derepress A3B and gain an evolutionary advantage.
source: This indicates that both virus-dependent and independent tumors may exploit the same pathway to derepress A3B and gain an evolutionary advantage.
evidence: This is inferred from the literature on HPV-positive and HPV-negative cancers.

claim: Breast cancer frequently has lesions in the RB/E2F pathway, including loss of RB1, CDKN1B (encoding p27), and CDKN2A as well as amplification of CCND1.
source: This possibility is also supported by frequent lesions in the RB/E2F pathway in breast cancer, including loss of RB1, CDKN1B (encoding p27), and CDKN2A as well as amplification of CCND1 (Angus et al., 2019; Bertucci et al., 2019; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2015; Ertel et al., 2010; Nik-Zainal et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Network, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: High levels of expression of a set of 20 normally E2F-repressed genes may be used to identify tumors with elevated levels of APOBEC signature mutations.
source: Our studies also raise the possibility that high levels of expression of a set of 20 normally E2F-repressed genes may be used to identify tumors with elevated levels of APOBEC signature mutations (Figure 6A–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is proposed based on the TCGA data analyses shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: Such information could be useful to help identify the subset of patients with hypermutated tumors that may be most responsive to immunotherapy.
source: Such information could be useful, for instance, to help identify the subset of patients with hypermutated tumors that may be most responsive to immunotherapy.
evidence: This is a speculative application of the findings.
